title: An order validator with its own and, or and negate

blocks.text: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, but it may carry any number of `default` and `static` methods. That is how a domain interface such as an order validator earns its place over a plain `Predicate<Order>`: its name says what it checks, and its own default methods let validators be combined.
`OrderValidator` declares the one abstract method `boolean validate(Order order)`, where `Order` is the record `Order(List<String> items, double total, String customer)`. Write its other methods:

items: `default OrderValidator and(OrderValidator other)`: valid when both are.
`default OrderValidator or(OrderValidator other)`: valid when at least one is.
`default OrderValidator negate()`: valid when this one is not.
`static OrderValidator hasItems()`: the order's item list is not empty, whatever its entries are and whatever the total.
`static OrderValidator hasCustomer()`: the order's customer is not `null` (a blank customer still counts).

blocks.text: A validator may be expensive, or may only be safe to run after an earlier one has passed: combine them the way `&&` and `||` combine conditions, not the way `&` and `|` do.

cases.says: Validators combine with and, or and negate; hasItems checks only that the list is non-empty, and hasCustomer only that the customer is not null.
and never runs the second check once the first has failed, just as && does.
or never runs the second check once the first has passed, just as || does.

concepts: A custom functional interface earns its place with domain meaning and its own composition methods; common cases use the standard ones.
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, and it may add default and static methods around it.
